igcse-0580-standard-form-large-numbers.description: Write large numbers as a coefficient multiplied by a power of ten. Expand positive exponents and check that the coefficient lies in the correct range.

sections.title: How do I recognise the two parts?
sections.label: The leading digit
sections.intro: Standard form writes a positive quantity compactly. The leading digit gives a scale for the whole number. The power of ten tells you how large that scale is.

blocks.html:
Write \(A\times10^n\) with \(1\le A<10\). Find \(A\) by putting the point after the first non-zero digit.

Original sizePower-of-ten factor
At least 10\(n>0\)
From 1 up to 10, excluding 10\(10^0=1\) (no shift)
Between 0 and 1\(n<0\)

figure.alt: The leading digit shifts three places from units to thousands.
figure.caption: For \(4.26\times10^3\) the digit 4 moves from units to thousands.

blocks.title: Write a large number in standard form
blocks.prompt: Write \(2\,370\,000\,000\) in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.
blocks.hint: Write one non-zero digit before the point. Count the place-value shift to recover the original.
blocks.solution:
Move the leading non-zero digit to the units place to find the coefficient \(2.37\).

To recover the original, multiply the coefficient by 10 a total of 9 times. The exponent is \(9\).

So \(2\,370\,000\,000=2.37\times10^{9}\).

retry.feedback: The original is greater than 10. Recover it by multiplying the coefficient by a positive power of ten.

blocks.html: The leading digit is the first non-zero digit. Zeros between significant digits belong to the coefficient.

blocks.title: Expand a positive power of ten
blocks.prompt: Write \(2.97\times10^{6}\) as an ordinary number.
blocks.hint: Expand the power of ten. Shift the digits into higher place values.
blocks.solution:
The positive exponent means multiply by \(10^{6}\).

Move the digits 6 places towards higher place values. Keep the digits in their original order.

This gives \(2\,970\,000\).

blocks.html: A coefficient of 10 is outside the permitted range. A coefficient of 1 is allowed.

sections.title: How can I go in either direction?
sections.label: Write and expand
sections.intro: Think about the shift from the coefficient back to the original. Moving digits towards higher places multiplies the value.

blocks.html: A positive exponent tells you how many places to move towards larger place values. Add zeros only where places need filling.

blocks.title: Write a large number in standard form
blocks.prompt: Write \(10\,310\) in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.
blocks.hint: Write one non-zero digit before the point. Count the place-value shift to recover the original.
blocks.solution:
Move the leading non-zero digit to the units place to find the coefficient \(1.031\).

To recover the original, multiply the coefficient by 10 a total of 4 times. The exponent is \(4\).

So \(10\,310=1.031\times10^{4}\).

retry.feedback: The original is greater than 10. Recover it by multiplying the coefficient by a positive power of ten.

blocks.html: Writing \(3.07\times10^4\) as 30 700 needs the zero between 3 and 7. Appending four zeros to 3.07 would leave the value unchanged.

blocks.title: Expand a positive power of ten
blocks.prompt: Write \(2.15\times10^{8}\) as an ordinary number.
blocks.hint: Expand the power of ten. Shift the digits into higher place values.
blocks.solution:
The positive exponent means multiply by \(10^{8}\).

Move the digits 8 places towards higher place values. Keep the digits in their original order.

This gives \(215\,000\,000\).

blocks.html: Check by converting your ordinary number back to standard form.

sections.title: How do I check and correct my standard form?
sections.label: Normalise the coefficient
sections.intro: Sometimes a question gives a numerical product with a power of ten that has an out-of-range coefficient. Keep the value while changing its two factors.

blocks.html: If you divide the coefficient by 10, multiply the power of ten by 10 to compensate. That raises the exponent by 1.

blocks.title: Report a survey length
blocks.prompt: A trail survey recorded \(3\,610\,000\) metres of marked trails across a region. Write the total length in metres in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.
blocks.hint: Write one non-zero digit before the point. Count the place-value shift to recover the original.
blocks.solution:
Move the leading non-zero digit to the units place to find the coefficient \(3.61\).

To recover the original, multiply the coefficient by 10 a total of 6 times. The exponent is \(6\).

So \(3\,610\,000\,\mathrm{m}=3.61\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}\).

retry.feedback: The original is greater than 10. Recover it by multiplying the coefficient by a positive power of ten.

blocks.html: Changing the coefficient and leaving the exponent alone changes the value.

blocks.title: Correct a coefficient that is too large
blocks.prompt: Rewrite \(42.1\times10^{10}\) in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.
blocks.hint: Compensate for dividing the coefficient by 10.
blocks.solution:
The coefficient \(42.1\) is too large. Divide it by 10 to obtain \(4.21\).

To keep the value unchanged, increase the exponent from \(10\) to \(11\).

\(42.1\times10^{10}=4.21\times10^{11}\).

retry.feedback: Reducing the coefficient by a factor of 10 requires a power of ten that is ten times as large.

blocks.html: Show the correction on your last line and keep any measurement unit in the answer.

To recover the original, multiply the coefficient by 10 a total of 4 times. The exponent is \(4\).

igcse-0580-standard-form-small-numbers.description: Read negative exponents, convert small decimals, compare their sizes and interpret a calculator exponent display.

sections.title: Why does a small positive number use a negative exponent?
sections.label: The first decimal place
sections.intro: A negative exponent of ten represents division by a power of ten. This is how a positive coefficient can name a positive value below 1.

blocks.html: \(10^{-3}=\frac{1}{1000}\). The first non-zero digit of \(0.00264\) sits in the third decimal place.

figure.alt: On a place-value strip the highlighted third decimal column is thousandths.
figure.caption: The leading digit in \(0.00264\) is in the thousandths column.

blocks.title: Convert a small decimal
blocks.prompt: Write \(0.000000399\) in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.
blocks.hint: Count from tenths, which is the first place after the decimal point.
blocks.solution:
Read the first non-zero digit and the digits that follow. They give \(3.99\).

The first non-zero digit stands 7 places after the decimal point.

Recover the smaller value by multiplying by \(10^{-7}\). Thus \(0.000000399=3.99\times10^{-7}\).

retry.feedback: A negative exponent makes the positive coefficient smaller.

blocks.html: A minus sign on the exponent does not make the value negative.

blocks.title: Convert a negative exponent to a decimal
blocks.prompt: Write \(4.55\times10^{-3}\) as an ordinary number.
blocks.hint: Keep the first non-zero digit in the decimal place given by the size of the exponent.
blocks.solution:
The negative exponent means divide \(4.55\) by \(10^{3}\).

Make sure its leading digit occupies the 3th place after the point.

The ordinary number is \(0.00455\).

blocks.html: The first decimal place is tenths. If the leading digit is in decimal place \(k\), the exponent is \(-k\).

sections.title: How do I correct a small coefficient or read E on a calculator?
sections.label: Repair and read displays
sections.intro: The digits before E on many calculators give a coefficient. The signed number after E tells the power of ten. Calculator key names differ.

blocks.html: Read \(2.64\mathrm{E}{-}3\) as \(2.64\times10^{-3}\). If the coefficient is below 1, raise it into range and decrease the exponent to compensate.

blocks.title: Correct a coefficient smaller than one
blocks.prompt: Rewrite \(0.0453\times10^{-9}\) in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.
blocks.hint: A coefficient increased by a factor of 100 needs a power-of-ten factor divided by 100.
blocks.solution:
Multiply \(0.0453\) by 100 to obtain \(4.53\).

To keep the number unchanged, undo this using a factor of \(10^{-2}\) in the power of ten.

\(0.0453\times10^{-9}=4.53\times10^{-11}\).

retry.feedback: The coefficient got larger. The power-of-ten factor needs to get smaller.

blocks.html: When you use an EXP, EE or equivalent key, it already introduces a power of ten. Enter only the signed exponent after it.

blocks.title: Read a calculator exponent display
blocks.prompt: A calculator displays \(5.09\mathrm{E}{-}5\). Write the number in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.
blocks.hint: E on this display introduces the power of ten.
blocks.solution:
Read the digits before E as the coefficient.

The signed number after E is the exponent. The display represents \(5.09\times10^{-5}\).

retry.feedback: Keep the minus sign on the calculator display.

blocks.html: In a written answer, replace the calculator's E display with the full power of ten.

sections.title: How can I count places or compare two small values?
sections.label: Zeros and comparisons
sections.intro: A digit’s position determines more than the appearance of its coefficient. Find the first occupied place before comparing any later digits.

blocks.html: The leading digit of \(A\times10^{-k}\) is in decimal place \(k\), so exactly \(k-1\) zeros occur after the point before it. For positive numbers in standard form, compare exponents first. Compare coefficients if the exponents match.

blocks.title: Count leading zeros without expanding
blocks.prompt: The number \(5.07\times10^{-3}\) is written as an ordinary decimal. How many zeros are there between the decimal point and the first non-zero digit?
blocks.hint: Count the positions before the first non-zero digit. Leave that digit out of the count.
blocks.solution:
The first non-zero digit appears in decimal place \(3\).

All \(2\) positions before that digit, after the decimal point, contain zeros.

blocks.html: A larger coefficient can still give the smaller number if its exponent is lower.

blocks.title: Compare two small numbers
blocks.prompt: Which value is greater, \(5.63\times10^{-7}\) or \(2.92\times10^{-7}\)? Give the greater value in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.
blocks.hint: Decide which leading digit occupies the higher place value.
blocks.solution:
The exponents match. Compare the coefficients.

The larger value is \(5.63\times10^{-7}\).

blocks.html: Keep both values in standard form when comparing. This saves writing a long string of zeros.

examples.title: Convert a small decimal
examples.question: Write \(0.00283\) in standard form.
solution: Read the first non-zero digit and the digits that follow. They give \(2.83\).
The first non-zero digit stands 3 places after the decimal point.
Recover the smaller value by multiplying by \(10^{-3}\). Thus \(0.00283=2.83\times10^{-3}\).

examples.title: Convert a negative exponent to a decimal
examples.question: Write \(3.39\times10^{-7}\) as an ordinary number.
solution: The negative exponent means divide \(3.39\) by \(10^{7}\).
Make sure its leading digit occupies the 7th place after the point.
The ordinary number is \(0.000000339\).

examples.title: Correct a coefficient smaller than one
examples.question: Rewrite \(0.0337\times10^{-5}\) in standard form.
solution: Multiply \(0.0337\) by 100 to obtain \(3.37\).
To keep the number unchanged, undo this using a factor of \(10^{-2}\) in the power of ten.

examples.title: Read a calculator exponent display
examples.question: A calculator displays \(3.93\mathrm{E}{-}9\). Write the number in standard form.
solution: Read the digits before E as the coefficient.
The signed number after E is the exponent. The display represents \(3.93\times10^{-9}\).

examples.title: Count leading zeros without expanding
examples.question: The number \(3.91\times10^{-7}\) is written as an ordinary decimal. How many zeros are there between the decimal point and the first non-zero digit?
solution: The first non-zero digit appears in decimal place \(7\).
All \(6\) positions before that digit, after the decimal point, contain zeros.

examples.title: Compare two small numbers
examples.question: Which value is greater, \(4.47\times10^{-3}\) or \(1.76\times10^{-3}\)? Give the greater value in standard form.
solution: The exponents match. Compare the coefficients.
The larger value is \(4.47\times10^{-3}\).

extraPractice.prompt: Rewrite \(0.0569\times10^{-5}\) in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.

To keep the number unchanged, undo this using a factor of \(10^{-2}\) in the power of ten.

\(0.0569\times10^{-5}=5.69\times10^{-7}\).

extraPractice.hint: E on this display introduces the power of ten.
extraPractice.solution:

The signed number after E is the exponent. The display represents \(6.25\times10^{-9}\).

retry.feedback: Keep the minus sign on the calculator display.

extraPractice.prompt: The number \(6.23\times10^{-7}\) is written as an ordinary decimal. How many zeros are there between the decimal point and the first non-zero digit?
extraPractice.hint: Count the positions before the first non-zero digit. Leave that digit out of the count.
extraPractice.solution:

extraPractice.prompt: Which value is greater, \(6.79\times10^{-3}\) or \(4.08\times10^{-3}\)? Give the greater value in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.
extraPractice.hint: Decide which leading digit occupies the higher place value.
extraPractice.solution:

Compact calculator notation for multiplying by a signed power of ten.

igcse-0580-standard-form-multiply-divide.description: Separate coefficient calculations from laws of indices, then normalise the result. Use the same steps for powers and practical questions.

sections.title: Why do the exponents add in a product?
sections.label: Multiply on two tracks
sections.intro: Group the ordinary coefficients together and the powers of ten together. The coefficient calculation and the exponent calculation have different rules.

blocks.html: Multiply the coefficients. Then apply \(10^m\times10^n=10^{m+n}\). Finally put the coefficient into the standard range.

figure.alt: Parallel coefficient and powers-of-ten tracks combine, with a final normalisation step.
figure.caption: Follow a separate track for the coefficient and the exponent.

blocks.title: Multiply two standard-form values
blocks.prompt: Work out \(\left(5.63\times10^{12}\right)\left(8\times10^{-6}\right)\). Give your answer in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.
blocks.hint: Keep coefficient work and power-of-ten work on separate lines. Check the coefficient before submitting.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the coefficients and add the exponents. This gives \(45.04\) and \(12+(-6)=6\).

The combined value before a final check is \(45.04\times10^{6}\). Adjust the coefficient by a power of ten and compensate in the exponent.

Write \(4.504\times10^{7}\).

retry.feedback: The intermediate value is right, but the coefficient still needs to be brought into the range from 1 up to, but excluding, 10.

blocks.html: Multiplying the exponents describes neither the size of the power-of-ten product nor its place-value shift.

blocks.title: Square a value in standard form
blocks.prompt: Work out \(\left(5.15\times10^{5}\right)^2\). Give your answer in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.
blocks.hint: Keep coefficient work and power-of-ten work on separate lines. Check the coefficient before submitting.
blocks.solution:
Square the coefficient and the power separately. Square \(5.15\) and use \((10^{5})^2=10^{10}\).

The combined value before a final check is \(26.5225\times10^{10}\). Adjust the coefficient by a power of ten and compensate in the exponent.

Write \(2.65225\times10^{11}\).

retry.feedback: The intermediate value is right, but the coefficient still needs to be brought into the range from 1 up to, but excluding, 10.

blocks.html: Show the intermediate coefficient if you still need to normalise it.

sections.title: Why does the denominator’s exponent get subtracted?
sections.label: Divide on two tracks
sections.intro: The quotient asks which factor would multiply the denominator back to the numerator. Subtracting exponents produces that factor.

blocks.html: Divide the coefficients and use \(\frac{10^m}{10^n}=10^{m-n}\). A negative denominator exponent needs brackets when you subtract it.

blocks.title: Divide two standard-form values
blocks.prompt: Work out \(\frac{3.28\times10^{13}}{2\times10^{-7}}\). Give your answer in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.
blocks.hint: Keep coefficient work and power-of-ten work on separate lines. Check the coefficient before submitting.
blocks.solution:
Divide the coefficients and subtract the denominator’s exponent from the numerator’s exponent. This gives \(1.64\) and \(13-(-7)=20\).

The combined value before a final check is \(1.64\times10^{20}\). The coefficient already satisfies \(1\le A<10\).

Write \(1.64\times10^{20}\).

retry.feedback: Apply the exponent rule for the operation in this question.

blocks.html: If the new coefficient is less than 1, raise that coefficient and lower the exponent. Do not lower both.

blocks.title: Divide two standard-form values
blocks.prompt: Work out \(\frac{1.48\times10^{4}}{5\times10^{-11}}\). Give your answer in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.
blocks.hint: Keep coefficient work and power-of-ten work on separate lines. Check the coefficient before submitting.
blocks.solution:
Divide the coefficients and subtract the denominator’s exponent from the numerator’s exponent. This gives \(0.296\) and \(4-(-11)=15\).

The combined value before a final check is \(0.296\times10^{15}\). Adjust the coefficient by a power of ten and compensate in the exponent.

Write \(2.96\times10^{14}\).

retry.feedback: The intermediate value is right, but the coefficient still needs to be brought into the range from 1 up to, but excluding, 10.

blocks.html: On a calculator, bracket a whole denominator when you type it with the division key.

sections.title: How do powers and practical questions use the same method?
sections.label: Powers and rates
sections.intro: Squaring is multiplying a number by itself. For a practical question, decide which operation gives the requested unit before touching the exponents.

blocks.html: Square both factors of a product. When finding a total, multiply the number of equal items by the amount per item. When finding an equal share, divide.

blocks.title: Find the capacity used by a sensor
blocks.prompt: A sensor saves \(5.27\times10^{4}\) bytes in each log. It saves \(5\times10^{3}\) logs during a trial. Find the total number of bytes stored. Give your answer in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.
blocks.hint: Keep coefficient work and power-of-ten work on separate lines. Check the coefficient before submitting.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the coefficients and add the exponents. This gives \(26.35\) and \(4+(3)=7\).

The combined value before a final check is \(26.35\times10^{7}\). Adjust the coefficient by a power of ten and compensate in the exponent.

Write \(2.635\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{bytes}\).

retry.feedback: The intermediate value is right, but the coefficient still needs to be brought into the range from 1 up to, but excluding, 10.

blocks.html: Squaring \(A\times10^n\) produces \(A^2\times10^{2n}\). Leaving the coefficient unchanged does not square the whole value.

blocks.title: Find the mass per test well
blocks.prompt: A laboratory shares \(2.65\times10^{-8}\) grams of powder equally between \(5\times10^{2}\) sealed test wells. Find the mass in grams in one well. Give your answer in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.
blocks.hint: Keep coefficient work and power-of-ten work on separate lines. Check the coefficient before submitting.
blocks.solution:
Divide the coefficients and subtract the denominator’s exponent from the numerator’s exponent. This gives \(0.53\) and \(-8-(2)=-10\).

revision.body:
Methods

StepWhat to do
Multiply on two tracksMultiply the coefficients. Then apply \(10^m\times10^n=10^{m+n}\). Finally put the coefficient into the standard range.
Divide on two tracksDivide the coefficients and use \(\frac{10^m}{10^n}=10^{m-n}\). A negative denominator exponent needs brackets when you subtract it.
Powers and ratesSquare both factors of a product. When finding a total, multiply the number of equal items by the amount per item. When finding an equal share, divide.

Worked conversion or calculation

\((4.6\times10^3)(3\times10^{-5})=1.38\times10^{-1}\)

Check yourself

Work out \(\frac{3.2\times10^{-4}}{8\times10^{-7}}\) in standard form.

Answer \(4\times10^2\)
revision.checks:
• Multiplying the exponents describes neither the size of the power-of-ten product nor its place-value shift.
  • If the new coefficient is less than 1, raise that coefficient and lower the exponent. Do not lower both.
  • Squaring \(A\times10^n\) produces \(A^2\times10^{2n}\). Leaving the coefficient unchanged does not square the whole value.
revision.examTip: At Core, calculations with standard form are assessed on Paper 3.

igcse-0580-standard-form-add-subtract.description: Align the powers of ten, add or subtract the coefficients and normalise the result, including calculations with very large exponents.

sections.title: Why must the powers of ten match?
sections.label: Use one shared scale
sections.intro: Adding or subtracting combines quantities measured in the same-sized units. A power of ten is the size of those units.

blocks.html: Rewrite one term to match the other. Keep the shared exponent while combining coefficients.

figure.alt: Two complete blocks and half a block use one shared unit size.
figure.caption: Rename quantities in matching power-of-ten units before adding or subtracting.

blocks.title: Add values in standard form
blocks.prompt: Work out \(\left(6.11\times10^{7}\right)+\left(6.02\times10^{7}\right)\). Give your answer in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.
blocks.hint: Make the powers the same before combining. You may also convert to ordinary numbers when the exponents are manageable.
blocks.solution:
Both terms already use \(10^{7}\).

Combine the coefficients and keep the shared exponent: \(\left(6.11+6.02\right)10^{7}=12.13\times10^{7}\).

Adjust the coefficient and compensate in the exponent. The result is \(1.213\times10^{8}\).

retry.feedback: The shared exponent is an intermediate step. Adjust it when you normalise your coefficient.

blocks.html: Adding exponents is a rule for multiplying powers. It does not add two scaled quantities.

blocks.title: Add values in standard form
blocks.prompt: Work out \(\left(4.95\times10^{9}\right)+\left(6.44\times10^{6}\right)\). Give your answer in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.
blocks.hint: Make the powers the same before combining. You may also convert to ordinary numbers when the exponents are manageable.
blocks.solution:
Use \(10^{9}\) as a shared scale. Rewrite the second term as \(0.00644\times10^{9}\).

Combine the coefficients and keep the shared exponent: \(\left(4.95+0.00644\right)10^{9}=4.95644\times10^{9}\).

The coefficient is already in range. The result is \(4.95644\times10^{9}\).

retry.feedback: Adding or subtracting values with a shared power keeps that power. Adding exponents applies to multiplication.

blocks.html: For manageable values, converting both to ordinary numbers is also a valid method.

sections.title: How do I subtract and check the size?
sections.label: Subtract and normalise
sections.intro: Check which quantity you are subtracting. Align the exponents and write the coefficient subtraction in the same order.

blocks.html: After subtracting, the difference can be much smaller than either original term. If the result is positive and the coefficient is below 1, shift it back up and decrease the exponent.

blocks.title: Subtract values in standard form
blocks.prompt: Work out \(\left(2.52\times10^{-11}\right)-\left(1.68\times10^{-13}\right)\). Give your answer in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.
blocks.hint: Make the powers the same before combining. You may also convert to ordinary numbers when the exponents are manageable.
blocks.solution:
Use \(10^{-11}\) as a shared scale. Rewrite the second term as \(0.0168\times10^{-11}\).

Combine the coefficients and keep the shared exponent: \(\left(2.52-0.0168\right)10^{-11}=2.5032\times10^{-11}\).

The coefficient is already in range. The result is \(2.5032\times10^{-11}\).

retry.feedback: Adding or subtracting values with a shared power keeps that power. Adding exponents applies to multiplication.

blocks.html: Do not subtract the two signed exponents. The matching exponent stays until the normalisation step.

blocks.title: Subtract values in standard form
blocks.prompt: Work out \(\left(5.89\times10^{-4}\right)-\left(5.74\times10^{-4}\right)\). Give your answer in standard form. Enter the coefficient and exponent of \(A\times10^n\) separately.
blocks.hint: Make the powers the same before combining. You may also convert to ordinary numbers when the exponents are manageable.
blocks.solution:
Both terms already use \(10^{-4}\).

Adjust the coefficient and compensate in the exponent. The result is \(1.5\times10^{-5}\).

retry.feedback: The shared exponent is an intermediate step. Adjust it when you normalise your coefficient.

blocks.html: If subtraction gives zero, write 0. No coefficient in the required positive range can represent zero.

sections.title: What if expanding the numbers would take too long?
sections.label: Big exponents and applications
sections.intro: Align powers directly instead of expanding a number with many zeros. Use a sensible shared power for the amount being measured.

blocks.html: To change from \(A\times10^{n-2}\) to a multiple of \(10^n\), divide the coefficient by 100. This is useful even when the powers are far beyond a calculator’s ordinary display.
